summary:
Ceuta, an autonomous city of Spain, stands under the national framework rather than under any regional statute of its own. Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Ceuta as elsewhere in Spain.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Courts are applying the aggravation in practice: a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300; in Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

Ceuta has no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute. The national index of autonomous-community LGTBI legislation states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla have no regional LGTBI statutes of their own and must instead apply the national equality framework and central-government policies. The gap is a statutory one: national criminal law and the national police operate in the city, so the enforcement floor available to a transgender visitor is the same as in the rest of the country.

FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, records Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. A 2020 precedent study had placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings. The report notes legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and records no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla.

Ceuta's border-fence context shapes the environment for LGTBI people there. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote by letter to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the mainland of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta.
tangentialFactors:
The absence of a regional statute in Ceuta is a comparative outlier within Spain rather than a national pattern: the national index of autonomous-community LGTBI legislation lists a law for each comunidad, and the FELGTBI+ radiography of September 2025 narrows the group of territories without a specific LGTBI+ promotion law to four, namely Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla. Castilla y León and Asturias legislated in June 2025; Ceuta and Melilla did not.

Ceuta shares its statutory-gap position with Melilla, the other autonomous city, and with Castilla y León as recorded in the 2025 inventory. A 2020 study ranking trans-student recognition and protection placed Ceuta and Melilla at the bottom of the table, which indicates the practical consequence of the gap for residents rather than for visitors subject to national law.

The border episode of 30 and 31 July, and Arcópoli's letter of 17 September 2026 to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, situate Ceuta as a point of irregular entry where LGTBI migrants arrive without documentation and with histories of criminalisation in their countries of origin. That context affects who is present in the city, how identity documents are handled, and what self-presentation is expected of people moving through the border zone.

Spain's national standing in comparative LGBT-friendliness rankings, together with same-sex marriage and adoption rights in force since 2005, provides the backdrop against which the Ceuta statutory gap should be read; the gap concerns regional promotion and protection instruments, not the national legal position.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ceuta have no regional LGTBI or gender-identity law to invoke. The national index of autonomous-community LGTBI legislation states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla must apply the national equality framework and central-government policies instead of a statute of their own, so claims for recognition, protection or services are brought under Ley 4/2023 and the national anti-discrimination provisions.

Trans students in Ceuta were ranked at the tail of recognition and protection tables in a 2020 study of trans-student policy, and the FELGTBI+ radiography of September 2025 records no legislative step for the city in the June 2025 round of reforms that advanced two other territories. Residents therefore continue to depend on central-government policy for school-level recognition.

Residents affected by the July border crossings can use the free remote social, psychological and legal support service opened by the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli for people in Ceuta, alongside the association's representation of their interests to the Secretary of State for Migration.

Trans residents use the administrative route at Article 43 of Ley 4/2023 to rectify the gender mention on their registry entry before the Civil Registry from age 16, with recognition possible from age 12 under conditions, and consent for medical procedures regulated for those aged 12 to 16.
outOfScopeNotes:
No incident evidence, no enforcement data and no hate-offence figure separating Ceuta from the national aggregate was retrievable from this inventory. The statutory gap is a statute-book finding, explicitly not a finding about violence or policing in the city.

Whether any court in Ceuta has applied the Article 22.4 transfobia aggravation is unresolved here; the two documented applications in the inventory come from Vigo and Valencia and are cited as evidence that the aggravation is used in practice nationally.

The 2020 trans-student recognition study is referenced through the FELGTBI+ radiography; its methodology, sample and full ranking are not sourced in this inventory.

The outcome of Arcópoli's letter of 17 September 2026 to the Secretary of State for Migration, including whether the requested transfers were authorised, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Whether Ceuta's autonomous-city institutions have adopted any policy instrument on gender identity or LGTBI matters under central-government frameworks, as distinct from a statute, is not addressed by the sources.
